disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) is characterized by an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (manic or mixed, and often depressive as well) concurrent with symptoms that meet Criterion A for schizophrenia. There must be at least a two-week period of psychotic symptoms (such as delusions or hallucinations) without prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features, while mood episodes are present for the majority of the total duration of the illness. The bipolar type features manic episodes and may include major depressive episodes across the course. The disorder typically leads to significant social and occupational impairment, and its course can be episodic with partial or full remissions, often complicated by stress, substance use, and nonadherence to treatment.

narrative.stressor: About fifteen months ago, Scott was promoted to take on more independent buying decisions just as his company pushed aggressive growth targets tied to upcoming sneaker drops. The combination of high stakes negotiations, long hours tracking global releases, and constant social media monitoring for trends blurred his work–life boundaries, and he began staying up later and taking impulsive solo trips to chase deals and art events. Over the year, his judgment at work became increasingly erratic—overcommitting to risky inventory, missing key deadlines, and clashing with colleagues and vendors—leading to formal performance warnings and tension with his manager. When he walked out mid‑shift to "pursue a vision" for a new line and refused to return, his parents and HR persuaded him to see a psychiatrist after they realized his behavior had been escalating and interfering with basic functioning for more than a year.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m on the verge of being a legendary visionary in fashion and everyone else is too small‑minded to keep up with me.”

narrative.stressor: Around a year and a few months ago, Alice and her spouse began seriously discussing starting a family while she was also taking on extra responsibilities training techs on new EV systems at the shop. The added pressure of planning for a future child, juggling overtime, and organizing church and car‑club commitments gradually strained her marriage; arguments over money, time at home, and her frequent late nights at the garage became more frequent. Over the following months, her coworkers and friends noticed unsettling changes in how she interpreted coworkers’ comments and how intensely she threw herself into projects, leading to conflicts with her supervisor and withdrawal from some social activities she once organized. After a particularly heated argument at home where her spouse expressed fear about how much she had "changed" and insisted something was wrong beyond normal stress, Alice agreed—reluctantly at first—to see a mental health professional at the recommendation of their pastor and primary care doctor.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep getting stuck on these ideas that people around me are plotting or judging me, even when they swear they aren’t.”

narrative.stressor: Fifteen months ago, Thomas’s long‑time executive retired and the company underwent a major reorganization, leaving him reporting to a new, younger leader while simultaneously taking on expanded coordination duties across multiple departments. The shift disrupted the structured routines he had cultivated for years and added evening events and cross‑time‑zone meetings that encroached on his art activities, hiking, and mentoring at the community center. Over the next year, colleagues saw his reliability and polished demeanor give way to disorganized scheduling, missed follow‑through on projects, and increasingly unusual comments during meetings, while at home his spouse noticed abrupt changes in his energy, sleep, and engagement with family and community events. After Thomas showed up unannounced at the office on a weekend insisting he needed to "document a hidden pattern" in company communications and his supervisor found him confused and unable to account for recent mistakes, HR contacted his spouse, who brought him to a psychiatric evaluation when it was clear his functioning had seriously deteriorated.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been seeing and hearing things at work and at home that no one else seems to notice, and it’s starting to scare me.”
